body.text: It is truism that maritime transportation is vital to the global economy. It carries over 80 percent of international trade and keeps essential goods moving. However recent disruptions in important waterways (such as the Black Sea, the Red Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Panama Canal) whether due to geopolitical tensions, security incidents, or climate-related challenges, have resulted in a sharp rise in maritime transportation costs and growing uncertainty for global supply chains.

As these risks grow, countries may reconsider their reliance on maritime chokepoints and many are actively looking for alternative ways to move goods. This has led to renewed interest in overland trade routes, especially across Eurasia, including the Middle Corridor, TRIPP, and the International North-South Transport Corridor.

One of the latest additions to the region’s list of connectivity projects that are currently on the table is the Central Asia-South Asia (CASA) railway. It represents a rail link from Central Asia to Pakistani seaports, passing through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. If realized, the CASA railway could tie Central Asia to Karachi, Port Qasim, and potentially Gwadar, offering a potential route to maritime markets in South Asia, the Persian Gulf, and East Africa.

However, the project is at a nascent stage. A memorandum signed by Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the UAE on September 30, 2026 makes no reference to the exact route, construction schedule, or projected cost. For now, the CASA railway remains an ambition rather than a concrete project, with its future tied to cargo volumes, transit tariffs, and the ability of the countries involved to reach agreement on infrastructure and cross-border procedures.
More than the Sum of its Parts

The countries involved are very much aware of this and are now turning to the practical requirements for increasing regional connectivity. In Kazakhstan, the focus is on what officials call the soft infrastructure of connectivity: digitalizing transport operations, moving paperwork online, and streamlining border procedures. Kazakhstan has already rolled out electronic exchanges of transport permits with Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan, and is promoting the idea of a “single digital corridor.”

In October 2026, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared 2027 the “Year of Nationwide Large-Scale Construction,” with the “People’s Construction” (Halyqtyq Qurylys) program being launched to modernize the country’s infrastructure. The Kazakh government has set out a plan to spend 6.5 trillion tenge (around $14.3 billion) from the National Fund by 2029. The initiative will be focused on the construction of essential social, transport, and engineering facilities, with the digitalization of the transport corridors and freight documentation also on the list.

Authorities have also taken steps toward accelerating digitalization and the adoption of AI solutions in the transport industry: Smart Cargo, Trip Optimizer, Kinetix, the National Video Control System, e-Joldar, Q-Gate, QazETA, among others. The Smart Cargo platform, in particular, enables online tracking of international cargo flows through a single-window system, so that moving goods doesn’t feel like navigating a maze.

The government’s push for digitalization is also being reflected in new appointments. The November 3 appointment of Assel Zhanassova as the new minister of transport, with the added status of deputy prime minister, drastically elevates the sector’s political profile. In addition, Zhanassova’s background in digitalization fits neatly with the authorities focus on technology.

Uzbekistan, for its part, is now pursuing a hub-and-corridor approach, with a view to creating a number of specialized logistics hubs, and associated transport corridors, coupled with customs reforms and the use of digital tools. All this is aimed to reinforce the country’s place in regional and international trade.

On October 12, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev adopted a new resolution on the development of the transport and logistics system (2026-2030). It is a package of measures that combines infrastructure investment with tax and customs incentives, as well as mandatory digitalization. This move is designed to attract investors and uplift Uzbekistan’s standing in regional logistics.

The Uzbek government has very ambitious targets: doubling transport services and attracting $9.1 billion in investment by 2030. With the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 strategy, authorities have pushed forward digitalization of transport operations, introducing electronic permits, the E-logistika platform and digital payments. These steps go hand in hand with attempts to overhaul railway management and bring more order to traffic flows.

While Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are both very much in the mode of trying to strengthen their own position through infrastructure development and improved regional transport links, the UAE is approaching the issue from another angle. Presumably, its decision to get on board with the CASA railway project is not simply tied to logistics or investment opportunities. The UAE might also be looking to combine its capital and its logistics expertise with its increasing interest in AI and digital technologies.

The UAE has made no secret of its ambition to become the global technology hub to diversify its economy, putting artificial intelligence and digital transformation at the heart of its development plans. This focus is especially relevant for transport, where AI and automation promise to streamline cargo and logistics, and make cross-border trade smoother.

The UAE has also been actively pursuing technology partnerships with Kazakhstan, with agreements in place on data centers, smart road technologies, AI-enabled urban infrastructure, and industrial infrastructure. Its move to join the CASA railway project might be a way to link its financial resources and tech expertise with Central Asia’s expanding transport networks.

Therefore, for Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, this partnership is a chance to tap into something more than outside investment and logistics expertise, into advanced digital tools. Whether these technologies will actually be put to use in the envisioned CASA railway is still an open question, but the UAE’s involvement clearly might bring a new technological layer to the project.
Afghanistan: The Crucial Link in the Chain

The countries involved in the project want better regional connectivity, which promises to benefit them all. But their different geographical positions and economic priorities mean that they see the proposed routes through their own lenses. This does not automatically signal political tension or disagreements. Instead, it shows how a single infrastructure project can mean very different things to each of the benefactors, depending on their contexts and needs.
Both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are deepening ties with Afghanistan, focusing on trade, investment, and infrastructure. However, they approach Kabul differently.

Uzbekistan is making the most of its border with Afghanistan, turning Termez into a gateway between Central and South Asia. Since 2025, Tashkent has been pushing the Termez Dialogue, a new cooperation framework that frames Afghanistan as a bridge linking the two regions. The International Trade Center in Termez is intended to boost cross-border commerce, while the Termez Cargo Center has been positioned as both a regional logistics hub and a main transit point for United Nations aid to Afghanistan. Beyond its own borders, Uzbekistan has participated in expanding the Hairatan-Mazar-i-Sharif railway, and has thrown its weight behind the proposed Trans-Afghan railway. Tashkent and Kabul also consider expanding cooperation in various other industries ranging from food processing to construction and energy. The logic here is pretty straightforward: Tashkent wants to secure a place for itself in whatever future emerges for Afghanistan.

At the same time, Kazakhstan, despite having no shared border with Afghanistan, has worked to strengthen regional connectivity via other means. The Kazakh authorities launched a series of initiatives, including the Kazakh-Afghan Business Forum in Astana in 2023 and the opening of trading houses in Herat in 2023 and Kabul in 2026. Kazakhstan has also expressed its intention to invest up to $500 million in the Torghundi-Herat railway project in western Afghanistan, formalized through a memorandum of understanding in July 2025. Participation in the Khaf-Herat railway project through Integra Construction KZ further expands Kazakhstan’s presence in Afghanistan’s infrastructure. Astana is also working to boost its regional standing through establishing the U.N. Regional Center for the Sustainable Development Goals for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty in June 2026.

These recent steps are promising. The main uncertainty, however, is still the exact route that the CASA railway will take. The project’s details remain under wraps for now, though there are a number of possible routes crossing Afghanistan that could be relevant: the western route, passing through Herat, Kandahar, and Spin-Boldak and the eastern route, starting from Termez to Naibabad and running on to Kharlachi, would have to go through mountainous terrain in Afghanistan. Each of those would have very different infrastructure requirements and implications for the parties involved. So, the real test will whether different actors can actually come to work together, in a sense trading individual short-term gains for collective progress.
